Case Study 1 — Why Japan Recycles More Than Most Countries: Lessons for India

Executive Summary

Japan combines the 3R hierarchy, strict source segregation, product-specific recycling laws and disciplined municipal collection. Its low-landfill performance depends on prevention, recycling and controlled incineration—not recycling alone.

Background

Limited landfill space, dense cities and long-term resource-conservation policy led Japan to build a ‘sound material-cycle society’ with strong household participation.

Strategy / Initiative

• Reduce → Reuse → Recycle • Detailed source segregation • Producer/consumer responsibility • Scheduled municipal collection • Controlled incineration with energy recovery

Impact & Results — Data

Recycling rate, FY2024

19.3%

Recycled municipal waste

7.38 Mt

Landfilled waste

3.06 Mt

Waste reduction rate

99.2%

SWOT Analysis

S

Strong segregation culture & clear laws

W

Complex rules; high system/incineration cost

O

More reuse, repair & advanced recovery

T

Ageing infrastructure; complex new waste streams

Comparison with India

India has EPR rules but uneven segregation and collection. Japan’s strongest lesson is predictable household segregation and accountability; India should also integrate informal waste workers.

Recommendations

Standardise segregation; strengthen take-back; expand public education; integrate waste pickers; prioritise reduction/reuse before end-of-pipe recycling.

Conclusion

Japan shows that successful waste management is a coordinated system of behaviour, law, infrastructure and producer responsibility.

References

METI 3R Policies; Japan Ministry of Environment FY2024 municipal-waste data; CPCB E-Waste Rules 2022.

Case Study 2 — Switzerland’s E-Waste Success Story

Executive Summary

Switzerland uses a mature producer-led take-back system financed through an advance recycling contribution. Consumers can return covered electronics through dealers and official collection points without a separate disposal fee.

Background

To safely recover valuable materials and control hazardous fractions, Switzerland created cooperative take-back organisations with clear equipment categories and certified recycling partners.

Strategy / Initiative

• Advance recycling contribution • Dealer + official collection network • Producer/importer cooperation • Certified recyclers • Data-protection requirements for returned devices

Impact & Results — Data

Swico operating since

1994

Equipment recycled, 2018

>46,000 t

Swico signatories

760

Separate return charge

None

SWOT Analysis

S

Convenient national take-back & stable finance

W

Administration and compliance costs

O

Critical-mineral recovery & refurbishment

T

Rapid turnover, battery risks, treatment costs

Comparison with India

India relies on portal-based EPR certificates. Switzerland’s advantage is convenient physical take-back. India can combine its digital EPR system with denser, consumer-friendly collection points.

Recommendations

Expand authorised drop-off points; make return simple; strengthen recycler audits; add data-security guidance; link EPR finance to collection infrastructure.

Conclusion

Convenience, pre-financing, producer cooperation and professional recycling make the Swiss model highly effective and transferable in parts to India.

References

Swico Recycling official system pages; CPCB E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 FAQ; CPCB EPR Portal.

Case Study 3 — India’s E-Waste Management Rules 2022

Executive Summary

The E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 came into force on 1 April 2023 and created a portal-based EPR system in which registered recyclers generate certificates used by producers to meet recycling obligations.

Background

Rapid electronics consumption created a growing e-waste stream. The 2022 framework expanded product coverage and shifted compliance toward digital registration, recycling targets and certificate tracking.

Strategy / Initiative

• CPCB portal registration • Producer recycling targets • Recycler-generated EPR certificates • Refurbishing certificates • Environmental compensation + audit provisions

Impact & Results — Data

Rules effective

1 Apr 2023

EEE items covered

106

FY2023–24 generation

1.254 Mt

FY2024–25 generation

1.398 Mt

SWOT Analysis

S

National digital EPR architecture

W

Informal-sector data and collection gaps

O

Formalisation & critical-mineral recovery

T

Certificate fraud / weak verification risk

Comparison with India

This is India’s national framework. Compared with Switzerland, digital compliance is stronger but consumer collection is less convenient; compared with Japan, household segregation is less institutionalised.

Recommendations

Strengthen audits; publish state/city dashboards; integrate informal collectors; expand collection in colleges/offices/housing societies; track actual material recovery.

Conclusion

The Rules modernise e-waste governance, but success depends on credible verification, convenient collection and safe formalisation of informal flows.

References

MoEFCC E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022; CPCB FAQ; CPCB EPR Portal; CPCB e-waste generation reports.

Case Study 4 — Pune’s SWaCH Model

Executive Summary

SWaCH is a cooperative of self-employed waste pickers created through collaboration between Pune Municipal Corporation and KKPKP. It integrates waste pickers into door-to-door segregated collection while preserving recyclable-value income.

Background

Waste pickers already recovered recyclable materials but often lacked recognition and stable access. Pune formalised their role instead of replacing them with a fully contractor-driven system.

Strategy / Initiative

• Door-to-door wet/dry collection • Waste-picker cooperative model • User-fee income + recyclable recovery • Municipal coordination • Decentralised composting/biogas pathways

Impact & Results — Data

PMC–SWaCH MoU

2008

Members in cited snapshot

2,300

Households serviced

378,419

Coverage

76 prabhags / 15 wards

SWOT Analysis

S

Inclusive livelihood + strong recycling incentive

W

Depends on segregation and user-fee payment

O

Replication + digital service management

T

Privatisation, low recyclable prices, poor segregation

Comparison with India

Unlike many Indian systems that leave waste pickers outside formal service delivery, Pune directly integrates them. This makes the model particularly relevant to other Indian cities.

Recommendations

Formal contracts and IDs; PPE/insurance; protect access to recyclables; municipal support for weak-income areas; annually measure diversion and worker income.

Conclusion

SWaCH proves that circular-economy systems can improve both environmental performance and livelihoods through organised inclusion.

References

Swachh Bharat Urban: Zero Garbage and SWaCH Model Solid Waste Management in Pune; PMC/SWaCH institutional case material.

Case Study 5 — Dell’s Circular Economy Strategy

Executive Summary

Dell applies circular-economy principles across product design, repair, refurbishment, material selection, take-back and recycling, aiming to keep products and materials in use for longer.

Background

Electronics create material and carbon impacts throughout their lifecycle. Manufacturers can reduce waste upstream through durability, repairability, recycled materials and recovery design.

Strategy / Initiative

• Design for durability • Repair + refurbishment • Material optimisation • Recycled/renewable materials • Design for disassembly • Consumer/business recovery services

Impact & Results — Data

India consumer recycling

Any-brand IT

2030 renewable-energy goal

75%

2040 renewable-energy goal

100%

Circularity scope

Design → recovery

SWOT Analysis

S

Manufacturer controls design & global recovery

W

Complex supply chain; participation needed

O

Modular design & closed-loop materials

T

Rapid innovation, supply risk, greenwashing risk

Comparison with India

India’s EPR rules make producers responsible for end-of-life outcomes. Dell illustrates how firms can go beyond certificate compliance by combining EPR with repair, refurbishment and take-back.

Recommendations

Set India-specific take-back/reuse targets; publish recovery metrics; expand retail/doorstep collection; design replaceable components; partner with authorised recyclers and trained collectors.

Conclusion

Dell demonstrates that circular electronics begin at design and continue through repair, reuse and responsible recovery—not only end-of-life recycling.

References

Dell Technologies India: Accelerating the Circular Economy; Responsible Recovery & Recycling; Dell ESG resources; CPCB EPR Portal.
